_comment: The models this client knows how to talk to, and WHICH GENERATION OF
PROMPTS each one was trained on.
Why a map and not a constant: a model answers in whatever schema its prompt
asks for. Send a version-1 model the version-2 prompt and nothing errors —
it just answers worse, on every puzzle, silently. That is exactly the
2026-07-18 regression, where the shipped prompt kept asking for the legacy
output/simulate_drag/PascalCase schema long after the LoRA had been
retrained on action: drag / drags[].
Hardcoding one generation makes that inevitable the moment a new model
trains on different prompts: updating the constants breaks every already-
published model, and not updating them breaks the new one. So each model
declares its generation here, captchakraken.prompts serves the matching
built-ins, and both keep working.
`latest` is what you get by default. Pin a specific model with
CAPTCHA_LORA_ADAPTER (or CAPTCHA_LORA_NAME for a served alias) — pinning is
opt-in, so the default download and the default prompt always move forward
together. That coupling is why moving `latest` to a generation-2 model is
safe here and would not have been before: a client that ships this file
reads prompt_version 2 from the same entry that named the weights. Clients
old enough to predate this file resolve from pinned_model.json instead and
never see `latest`, so they are not silently moved onto prompts they cannot
produce.
Adding a model: add its entry here IN THE SAME COMMIT as publishing it. A
release gate fails if any registered model names a prompt_version this
client ships no built-ins for, so an unmapped model cannot reach a release.
`pixel_budget` is the same idea for RESOLUTION. Qwen reads MIN_PIXELS /
MAX_PIXELS from the environment and clamps each image's AREA into that band,
so it decides how many visual tokens the model reads a puzzle from. One
visual token is a 32x32 px square (patch_size 16, then spatial_merge_size 2).
It lives here, per model, for exactly the reason prompt_version does — one
client constant cannot be right for two adapters with different budgets.
SERVE-AT, not trained-at. Seed it from the training run, then tune it by
measurement: these adapters generalize UPWARD, so the best serving band is
usually larger than the training floor. Serving under a band nobody checked
is the prompt bug in a different costume — nothing errors, the model just
answers on a picture at a scale it was not tuned for.
Omit it and the client keeps its historical behaviour (floor at 448 squared,
no ceiling). Absent means UNKNOWN, not zero — set it only where it has been
measured or the training run is known.
`availability` says whether the WEIGHTS are obtainable. Two values:
"public"   — on the Hub; anyone may download and self-host it. This is
the default when the field is absent, so every entry that
predates the field keeps its meaning exactly.
"licensed" — NOT downloadable by anyone. Reachable only through
api.captchakraken.com, or by a holder of a licence we issue.
There is no Hub repo to point CAPTCHA_LORA_ADAPTER at, and
`captchakraken fetch` refuses rather than 404ing at the Hub.
Why it lives HERE and not only in a policy doc: this file is already the one
place that decides what an unpinned client downloads and what prompts it
sends. A second list of 'models you may not publish' kept somewhere else
would be a list that drifts, and the drift is silent in the direction that
costs the most. The finetune repo's publisher reads this field and REFUSES
to upload a licensed model to the Hub; check_prompt_parity.py refuses to let
`latest` be one, because an unpinned self-hoster would resolve to weights
they cannot obtain.
`experts` is the fourth axis, and the newest. A ROUTED model is not one
adapter: Abyss is four LoRAs behind one endpoint, and the thing that picks
between them is the PROMPT FAMILY the request is about to send — grid,
pixel, video, text. See docs/MOE_LORA_DESIGN.md §11: the router is the
prompt family and it already exists, so no DOM access, no image classifier
and no cooperation from the caller is needed to reach the right expert.
It lives here for the same reason prompt_version does. WHICH EXPERTS EXIST
IS A FACT ABOUT THE MODEL. A client that hardcoded four names would send
them to v1.2 — which serves one adapter under one name — and every request
would 404 on a model the endpoint has never heard of. ABSENT MEANS NOT
ROUTED, and that is the whole backwards-compatibility story: every model
published so far declares no `experts`, so the client sends the single
`lora_name` on every request exactly as it did before this field existed.
An unmapped or unrecognised family degrades to the model's own
`lora_name` — the GENERALIST — never to another expert and never to an
error. The day the generation-2 `text` family reached ckgate without a
marker, refusing it cost every distorted-text solve in production for a
day; a caller prompting in their own words is the expected case for a
shipped model, not a 400.
Each expert name must resolve — through `served_aliases` or as a repo id —
to a REGISTERED entry declaring the same `prompt_version` and the same
`pixel_budget` as the model that routes to it. check_prompt_parity.py
enforces that. It is what makes aliasing four arms onto one entry safe
rather than convenient: the four share a base, a schema and a band today
(measured, not assumed — runs 20260906-0142xx all carry prompt generation
2 and a flat 518400 band), and the day one of them trains at a different
generation or a different band the gate refuses the alias and that arm has
to graduate to an entry of its own. A divergence that resolved silently
through a shared entry would be the 2026-07-18 regression with four models
in it instead of one.
The four arms are on the wire training as this is written (runs
20260906-0142xx) and none of them is published yet, so the `experts` map
below names weights that do not exist. That is the same deliberate
arming as `Abyss` itself — registered before it existed so the licence
gates were armed rather than retrofitted — and it costs nothing, because
an expert name only ever reaches the wire for a caller who asked for a
routed model in the first place.

CaptchaKraken/CaptchaKraken-Lora-v1.2.note: PUBLIC on the Hub under Source-Available License v1.1, and the first published generation-2 model. TRAINED with floor 448^2 / ceiling 720^2, but MEASURED best served at a flat 720^2 — floor == ceiling, so every image arrives at exactly one size and the band cannot drift. The band was chosen by sweeping the serving floor over 448/576/640/704/720/736/768/896/1024^2 and scoring each arm: the plateau is 704-736^2, and it falls off above 768^2, where a 400x580 portrait capture runs more than 40% past the ViT's 48x48 position grid. Do not "just use the ViT's native grid": 640^2 is where that grid is exactly saturated for a portrait capture, and it scores WORSE than 720^2 — mild position-embedding extrapolation plus real pixels beats staying inside the grid. Was served as `captcha-v12` while absent from this file, which resolved it to generation 1 prompts against generation-2 weights — the failure this file exists to prevent.

CaptchaKraken/Twilight-v1.2-FP8.note: CaptchaKraken-Lora-v1.2 merged into Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B at FP8-dynamic. The weights the hosted API answers with. Generation 2, same band as the adapter it is made from: a merge that resolved to a different prompt generation or a different pixel budget than its own LoRA would be the 2026-07-18 regression with extra steps.

CaptchaKraken/Sunlight-v1.2-AWQ-4bit.note: CaptchaKraken-Lora-v1.2 merged into Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B at AWQ 4-bit. Generation 2. Quantization changes the weights, not the schema they answer in, so the prompt generation and the pixel budget are the adapter's.

CaptchaKraken/CaptchaKraken_v1.1.note: Currently served in production. PRIVATE on the Hub, so prompts.json can never be fetched for it — this entry is the only thing that maps it to a prompt generation.

CaptchaKraken/CaptchaKrakenV1_Lora.note: Published before prompts.json existed — no such file in the repo, so it resolves from here.

CaptchaKraken/Sunlight-AWQ-4bit.note: Ships its own prompts.json; this entry keeps it resolvable offline.

CaptchaKraken/Twilight-FP8.note: Ships its own prompts.json; this entry keeps it resolvable offline.

CaptchaKraken/Abyss.note: IN DEVELOPMENT. Never published, never downloadable — see `availability`. Registered before it exists so the licence gates are armed rather than retrofitted after the first artifact is sitting on a disk: the publisher, the parity gate and `captchakraken fetch` all read this entry, and a rule added the day it is first needed is a rule that was absent on the day it was first needed. Being nameable is not being downloadable: `availability` is what refuses the weights, and the two are independent on purpose — a licence holder DOES name this model, which is why it and each of its experts has a served_aliases entry. ABYSS IS THE ROUTED 9B, NOT THE 27B. It was going to be a single Qwen3.8-27B adapter; that model was trained (run 20260903-235101) and did not earn its cost, so the product became the four-expert mixture on Qwen3.5-9B that docs/MOE_LORA_DESIGN.md §7 and §10 specify. A routed 27B may be a later generation of this same name; it would be a new entry when it exists, because the base model is what a self-hoster loads. `lora_name` is `abyss-general` rather than a fifth name: the generalist IS the fallback for any family `experts` does not map, so pointing the two at one adapter is what makes §11’s “degrade to the generalist, never 400” true with one fewer resident LoRA slot — and slots are the binding constraint (§10, five names against `--max-loras`). prompt_version 2 and the flat 518400 band are what all four arms are training at TODAY (verified against training_runs/20260906-0142xx/run.json, min_pixels == max_pixels == 518400); CONFIRM BOTH from the run records at publish time and re-record here in the publishing commit, and if any arm has diverged give that arm its own entry — check_prompt_parity.py refuses the shared alias rather than resolving it silently.

served_aliases._comment: A hosted endpoint serves a bare name, not a repo id. Map it back so prompt resolution works for callers who only ever see the alias. api.captchakraken.com now serves ONE model behind the permanent public name `captcha`, whatever the caller sends, so `captcha` means whichever adapter is current there — today CaptchaKraken-Lora-v1.2 — and NOT the v1.1 weights that share the name as a local vLLM alias. Self-hosters resolve by repo id via CAPTCHA_LORA_ADAPTER and are unaffected. Move this in the same change as the gateway's CKGATE_UPSTREAM_MODEL or the hosted model answers a prompt generation it was not trained on.
served_aliases._comment_abyss: `abyss` is here for the OPPOSITE reason to the two above, and it is not a contradiction of `availability: licensed`. An alias says which model a served NAME means; availability says whether its weights can be downloaded. A licence holder does name this model — the hosted API accepts it from a licensed key and lists it to them on /v1/models so their SDK can — and without this line `canonical_model_id('abyss')` is None, so their prompts resolve through the `latest` fallback: the exact model/generation mispairing this file exists to prevent, silent, and only accidentally right while `latest` happens to share the generation. It does NOT make the weights fetchable; `captchakraken fetch` reads availability and refuses this name, which is also the clear error a self-hoster who typed it deserves.
served_aliases._comment_abyss_experts: The four expert arms. These are the names that go ON THE WIRE — a routed request for a grid names `abyss-grid`, never `abyss` — so without these lines `canonical_model_id` returns None for the string the client actually sent, and prompt resolution falls through to the `latest` fallback on every routed solve. That is the mispairing `abyss` itself is here to prevent, one level down and four times over. Aliasing four arms onto one entry rather than giving each its own is deliberate and CHECKED: they share a base, a prompt generation and a pixel band today, and check_prompt_parity.py requires every expert name to resolve to a registered entry declaring the SAME prompt_version and pixel_budget as the router — so the day an arm trains at another generation or another band, the gate refuses the alias and that arm has to graduate to an entry of its own.
